query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of silicon into boride-based components via powder metallurgy will form an in‐situ silicide barrier during hot-dip aluminum plating, thereby improving the resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard boride-based component without silicon addition.
generation.intervention: Alloy the boride material with a minor, controlled concentration of silicon (using powder metallurgy processing) so that during exposure to molten aluminum, a silicon-rich protective interfacial layer is formed.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating conditions (~660°C) for standard immersion durations. The intervention is expected to be effective provided the silicon concentration remains within an optimal range that avoids secondary phase formation or degradation of other essential material properties.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an in-situ, continuous silicide (or Al–Si enriched) interfacial barrier layer at the component surface.
generation.mechanism: During the hot-dip process, the silicon in the alloy reacts with aluminum to form a stable silicide layer. This layer acts as a barrier that inhibits further aluminum penetration and corrosion of the underlying boride structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The silicon-doped boride will exhibit a significantly reduced corrosion rate when immersed in molten aluminum compared to its undoped counterpart, as evidenced by slower degradation and improved microstructural integrity.
generation.baseline: Corrosion resistance of the conventional boride-based component without silicon addition under identical molten aluminum exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated to hold under standard hot-dip plating conditions (around 660°C and typical immersion durations). Deviations in temperature, exposure time, or silicon concentration outside the optimal range might negate the protective effect.
generation.uncertainty: While related studies in high-temperature corrosion systems suggest that minor silicon additions can enhance oxidation and corrosion resistance, the precise concentration range and magnitude of improvement for boride-based components in molten aluminum remain to be calibrated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride samples using powder metallurgy: one set with a controlled minor addition of silicon and one standard (control) set without silicon. Subject both sets to identical immersion in molten aluminum at 660°C for fixed time intervals. Post exposure, perform corrosion rate measurements and microstructural analysis (e.g., using SEM and XRD) to assess the formation of interfacial layers.
measurements: Corrosion rate (e.g., weight loss or depth of corrosion penetration)
Microstructure and phase identification of the surface/interface (using SEM, TEM, or XRD)
Uniformity and continuity of the silicide barrier layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the silicon-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate and lack evidence of a continuous silicide barrier layer compared to control samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

SP-FCC solid solutions were successfully synthesized in Al60Mg40 and Al50Mg50 (with λ ≤ 0.11), while the formation of a SP-FCC structure is unattainable in Al40Mg40Li10Zn10 alloy within the pressure range of 5-40 GPa up to 2000 K (corresponding to λ values greater than 0.11). This paper focuses on the microstructure, phase composition, mechanical, tribological and corrosion properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the CoCrCuFeNi system depending on copper content, which was varied from 0 to 20 at. % with an increment of 5%. CoCrCuFeNi alloys were manufactured by powder metallurgy methods: mechanical alloying and hot pressing of element mixtures. The solubility limit of copper in CoCrFeNi solid solution was found to be 9 at. %. Segregation of irregularly shaped copper grains sized 1–30 μm is observed at concentrations above this solubility limit. As copper concentration increases, the phase composition of CoCrCuFeNi alloys changes from the single phase based on FCC1 solid solution (Cu = 0–5 at. %) to the dual-phase FCC1 + FCC2 alloy (Cu = 10–20 at. %), where FCC1 is the main phase and FCC2 is the secondary copper-rich phase. Tribological tests have shown that doping the CoCrFeNi alloy with copper increased wear resistance by 23% due to solid solution hardening. chosen.why: This intervention directly addresses the open question by proposing a single, composition‐based change in the boride component. Doping with silicon is hypothesized to promote an in-situ formation of a protective silicide or Al–Si-rich interfacial barrier that limits molten-aluminum corrosion. Prior studies in related high-temperature corrosion systems support that a minor Si addition can enhance oxidation and corrosion resistance. A controlled experiment comparing standard versus Si-doped boride specimens under identical molten aluminum exposure conditions can validate or falsify this mechanism.
